data.text/html:
Normalization vs Standardization: an explorable lesson

Based on DataMListic: Normalization vs Standardization - Explained. Feature scaling is just a shift plus a stretch. In this notebook you move points, run gradient descent and add outliers to see why it matters and which scaler to choose. Color language used throughout: purple = raw data · blue = min-max normalization · orange = z-score standardization · red = outliers / the minimum we are looking for

data.text/markdown:
1. The scale problem: income is louder than age

The video's running example: predict something about a person from age (about 25 to 52) and income (45,000 to 200,000).
feature range
age ≈ 27
income ≈ 155,000 (≈ 6,000× larger)
Many algorithms quietly assume that bigger numbers mean more importance. Without scaling, the model hears income shouting and barely notices age. That is not because age is irrelevant. Income is simply measured in bigger units. The cost shows up in the loss landscape. With mismatched scales the loss contours become long, thin ellipses instead of circles. Gradient descent follows the steepest slope, so it zig-zags across the narrow valley and creeps along the long one. For a quadratic loss ||(L(w) = \tfrac12\,(w_1^2 + \kappa\, w_2^2)||), the stretch factor ||(\kappa||) grows like (scale ratio)².

Watch the zig-zag across the narrow (income) direction and the crawl along the age direction.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eDrag κ down to \u003cstrong\u003e1\u003c/strong\u003e. That is what scaling does. The ellipses become circles and the path goes straight to the red minimum.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eWith κ = 1, set the step to 1.0. It converges in a \u003cstrong\u003esingle step\u003c/strong\u003e. With a large κ, no step size helps both directions at once.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
2. Min-max normalization: squeeze everything into [0, 1]

||[x' = \frac{x - x_{\min}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}||]
  • The numerator shifts everything so the smallest value lands at 0.
  • The denominator rescales so the largest value lands at 1.
Every feature is guaranteed to live in ||([0, 1]||). It is clean and intuitive, and you always know where your data ends up. Below, the purple dots are incomes in thousands. The blue dashed lines mark min and max, the two numbers this scaler uses.

Only its own blue dot moves. Now drag the \u003cstrong\u003elargest\u003c/strong\u003e dot. \u003cem\u003eEvery\u003c/em\u003e blue dot moves, because the max is part of every row's formula.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eDrag the max far to the right (≈ 250). If two dots are twice as far apart as two others in purple, the same holds in blue.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
3. Z-score standardization: center at 0, one unit = one σ

||[x' = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}||]Subtract the mean μ and divide by the standard deviation σ. For the video's income data μ ≈ 103,800 and σ ≈ 53,800. After the transform the data is centered at 0 and has σ = 1, whatever the original units were. A value of ||(x' = 2||) simply means "two standard deviations above average". Same dots as before. The orange triangle is μ and the shaded band is μ ± σ, which maps to [−1, 1] below.

data.text/markdown:
Misconception: "standardizing makes my data normal"

It does not. Standardization is a linear transformation: a shift and a rescale. The shape of the distribution stays exactly the same. A skewed feature stays skewed and a bimodal feature stays bimodal. Pick a shape and compare.

data.text/markdown:
4. The outlier test

So which one should you use? The video says: it comes down to outliers. Take a well-behaved feature with values roughly in 0–100 and add one extreme value, say 500.
  • Min-max: the outlier becomes the new max and stretches the range enormously. All regular data gets compressed near 0 and loses most of its resolution.
  • Z-score: the outlier drags μ and σ a bit, but the result is not boxed into [0, 1]. The outlier just shows up far from the center.
Predict first: after adding the 500 and applying min-max, what fraction of the [0, 1] interval will the 40 regular points cover?
Make your guess, then lock it in to reveal the answer.

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eToggle the outlier off and on. In the blue strip the regular ticks collapse into a sliver near 0. In the orange strip they keep a usable spread.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ePush the outlier to 1000. Min-max gets worse and worse. Z-score also compresses, but more slowly, because σ grows only about linearly with one extreme value.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHonest footnote:\u003c/strong\u003e both scalers are linear, so neither is truly outlier-proof. The grey \u003cem\u003erobust\u003c/em\u003e row uses median and IQR, which one outlier barely moves (sklearn's \u003ccode\u003eRobustScaler\u003c/code\u003e).\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
5. Two sides of the same coin

Both methods are the same idea. Each is a linear map ||(x' = a\,x + b||):
scale ||(a||) shift ||(b||) output
min-max ||(1/(x_{\max}-x_{\min})||) ||(-x_{\min}/(x_{\max}-x_{\min})||) always in [0, 1]
z-score ||(1/\sigma||) ||(-\mu/\sigma||) mean 0, σ 1, unbounded
Order, relative spacing and distribution shape stay intact. What changes is what the algorithm sees: a fair representation in which no feature shouts because of its units. That matters most for algorithms that use distances (k-NN, k-means, SVM) or gradients (linear and logistic regression, neural nets). Tree-based models split one feature at a time on thresholds, so they barely care. Below, pick a person from the age/income table and see who their nearest neighbor is under each view.

data.text/markdown:
6. Sandbox: both scalers at once

Pick a preset, then drag, add (double-click the top axis) or remove (double-click a dot) points. The blue and orange rows update live. Challenges:
  • Make the min-max and z-score rows look identical in spacing. (They always are! Only the axis labels differ.)
  • Create a data set where z-score values reach beyond ±3.
  • Find out how few points you need before one point pins min-max to 1 while its z is only ≈ 1.

data.text/markdown:
Recap

Min-max normalization Z-score standardization
formula ||(x' = \dfrac{x - x_{\min}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}||) ||(x' = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}||)
output always in [0, 1] mean 0, σ 1, unbounded
uses min & max (2 extreme points) μ & σ (all points)
outliers one outlier squashes the rest near 0 handles them more gracefully (use robust scaling for heavy outliers)
shape of distribution unchanged unchanged (not made normal)
good for naturally bounded data (pixels, percentages) data with outliers; distance- and gradient-based models
Shared core: both are linear maps ||(x' = a x + b||). They shift and rescale, keep order and shape, and give each feature a fair voice, so gradient descent gets round contours and k-NN looks at every feature.
